extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners and patent practitioners evaluating 35 U.S.C. §101 subject-matter eligibility for life-science claims
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for analyzing life-science patent claims under the two-step (Step 2A/2B) subject-matter eligibility framework (2014 IEG): determine statutory category, identify judicial exceptions (product of nature / abstract idea), compare to closest naturally occurring counterpart for 'markedly different characteristics', and assess whether additional elements amount to 'significantly more'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory category determination (Step 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim is directed to a statutory category (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter) under 35 U.S.C. §101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim recites matter (e.g., a composition, gel, granular particles, controlled release formulation), treat it as a composition of matter and proceed to the judicial-exception analysis. Example: a claimed dietary sweetener composed of texiol and water is a 'composition of matter.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify if claim is directed to a judicial exception (Step 2A)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze whether the claim, viewed as a whole, is directed to a judicial exception (product of nature, law of nature, abstract idea).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For nature-based claims ask whether the claim as a whole is directed to a product of nature; for process claims ask whether the claimed steps (e.g., comparing sequences) recite an abstract idea. Use the claim's focus and high-level recitation to identify the exception. Example: a high-level comparing step was treated as an abstract idea in Myriad CAFC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-of-nature analysis via closest naturally occurring counterpart and 'markedly different characteristics'
rubrics_metrics.description: For nature-based products, compare the claimed subject matter to its closest naturally occurring counterpart to determine whether it has 'markedly different characteristics' from that counterpart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for changes in structure, function, or other properties that are relevant to the invention (e.g., organoleptic properties, physical form, dissolution rate, time-release behavior). If the claimed product has such markedly different characteristics, it is not a product-of-nature exception. Examples: (eligible) gel with improved mouthfeel and spreadable solid form; formulation with altered time-release properties; granular texiol with specific particle-size distribution producing increased, consistent dissolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI) in identifying natural counterparts
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpret the claim under the broadest reasonable interpretation to determine whether it covers a naturally occurring material or mixture and thus the relevant natural counterpart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply BRI to claim language (e.g., % texiol + water) to see if it encompasses naturally occurring sap; the BRI affects which natural counterpart is the proper comparison for the marked-differences analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marked differences must be relevant to the nature of the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Any altered property relied upon to show 'markedly different characteristics' should be relevant to the invention's purpose or nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the changed property (e.g., jelly-like spreadability, prolonged sweetness, improved dissolution) is meaningful to the invention (e.g., a dietary sweetener). If so, that supports eligibility (Claim 3, 4, 5, 6 examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixture analysis: consider components as additional elements to each other
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim recites a mixture of products of nature, consider each component as an additional element to the other(s) to assess whether the combination results in markedly different characteristics or significantly more than the components themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if components are products of nature, their combination may produce new properties. Conversely, if mixing does not change structure/function and was routine/conventional, the mixture may remain an ineligible product of nature. Example: mixing texiol and water in routine ways did not produce marked differences (Claim 2), but adding Compound N that altered organoleptic profile did (Claim 3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract-idea identification for high-level information-processing steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that recite high-level steps of collecting, comparing, or analyzing information (e.g., comparing a patient sequence to wild-type) can be directed to an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the recited comparison or mental steps impose no limits on how the comparison is performed, they are likely abstract. Narrowing the information compared (e.g., BRCA1 sequences) does not by itself make the claim non-abstract. Example: comparing BRCA1 sequences was treated as an abstract idea in the Myriad CAFC analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B: Determine whether additional elements individually or as an ordered combination amount to 'significantly more'
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim is directed to a judicial exception at Step 2A, analyze whether the additional elements (or their combination) add significantly more to the exception, rendering the claim eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether recited elements are unconventional or provide a specific, technical improvement beyond the exception. Example: reciting SNOM detection or Cool-Melt PCR (unconventional data-gathering or technique) can render a claim eligible at Step 2B because these elements are not routine or conventional in the field at the time of filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-understood, routine, and conventional exclusion for 'significantly more'
rubrics_metrics.description: An additional element that is well-understood, routine, and conventional in the field does not qualify as 'significantly more' to transform an exception into eligible subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should evaluate whether a recited technique was actually routine/conventional at the time of the invention. The mere physicality of additional elements (e.g., hybridizing step) does not confer eligibility if the technique is conventional (Alice Corp. v. CLS Bank principle). Example: autoradiography was conventional for detecting hybridization; SNOM was not widely used then and thus could be non-conventional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity of amounts/ratios alone is insufficient without demonstrated marked differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Reciting specific percentages, amounts, or ratios (e.g., 1–5% texiol, at least 90% water) does not by itself render a claim eligible unless those specifics produce or evidence marked differences from natural counterparts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If claimed numeric ranges are routine or do not change structure/function, they won't save eligibility. Best practice: explain which characteristics are markedly different and why, rather than relying only on numerical specificity (Claim 2 discussion).

rubrics_metrics.name: When to stop after Step 2A
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim is found not directed to any judicial exception at Step 2A (i.e., it has markedly different characteristics), the Step 2B analysis is not required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner may add remarks or reasons for allowance indicating the claim is not directed to a judicial exception, but need not perform the significantly-more considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection drafting guidance for examiners
rubrics_metrics.description: When rejecting a claim under §101, clearly identify the exception(s) and explain why the claim is directed to that exception and why additional elements do not render it eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point to the nature-based product or abstract-idea limitation, explain lack of marked differences or why mixing is routine/conventional, and, if helpful, cite and explain analogous case law (e.g., Roslin, Funk Brothers, Myriad, Alice) showing how the claim is similar to precedent. Example language: identify nature-based product (texiol-water), explain it is a product of nature, and explain absence of additional elements that add significantly more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and citation of analogous case law
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners may cite and explain how the claimed subject matter is analogous to prior court decisions addressing eligibility (e.g., Myriad, Roslin, Funk Brothers, Alice, Funk Brothers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If citing cases, include an explanation of how the claimed mixture or method is like the cited case (e.g., lack of markedly different characteristics, routine combination, or abstract comparison). Examples in text: compare claimed mixtures to Roslin or Funk Brothers to show lack of marked differences; compare information-comparison claims to Myriad/Ambry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate whether a claimed change is the result of a change in form/structure or mixing with other substances
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether alterations asserted (e.g., controlled release behavior, encapsulation, crystallization to regular particle sizes) arise from a change in form/structure or from mixing with other substances and whether those alterations produce marked differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: encapsulation in polymer-emulsifier mixtures that delay release (controlled release) or controlled crystallization/granulation producing regular particle-size distributions that increase dissolution are cited as changes in form/structure that support eligibility (Claims 5 and 6).

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus-of-claim consideration: do not perform product-of-nature analysis when claim is focused on process/abstract idea
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim's focus is on an informational or process step (e.g., comparing sequences), there is no need to perform the marked-differences analysis on recited nature-based products in that claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine claim focus: if the claim is directed to an abstract idea/process, treat the exception analysis accordingly (see Claim 1 gene comparison example where the comparing step was the focus and treated as abstract).
